::: {.callout-note}
## Executive Summary
This project goes beyond "train a churn classifier and report accuracy." It answers a retention team's actual question — not just who will churn, but what's the dollar-optimal way to spend a limited retention budget on them — using real data from 7,043 telecom customers, RFM-style segmentation, a compared pair of models, and a per-customer cost-optimized decision threshold.
:::

## The Core Finding

A cost-optimized retention threshold saves **$283,589** versus doing nothing, and a further **$73,319** versus the textbook-default 0.50 cutoff — on a 1,761-customer held-out test set alone.

| Strategy | Total Cost | Savings vs. Do-Nothing |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Do Nothing | $411,785 | — |
| Standard Threshold (0.50) | $201,515 | $210,270 |
| Cost-Optimized Threshold (τ=0.14) | $128,196 | $283,589 |

## Methodology

Two models — Logistic Regression and Random Forest — were trained on a stratified 75/25 train/test split and compared by ROC-AUC on the held-out set. The higher-AUC model's predicted probabilities drive the cost-optimization analysis.

Unlike a flat cost matrix, each customer's false-negative cost is **their own annual revenue at stake** (monthly charge × 12) — a more realistic model of what a retention team actually loses per missed churner, since losing a $30/month customer and a $100/month customer are not equally costly mistakes.

Customer segments were built via KMeans clustering on tenure (loyalty proxy), number of subscribed services (engagement proxy), and monthly charge (value proxy) — an RFM-style approach adapted for a subscription business rather than a transactional one.

Full SQL/Python source is in the project's [GitHub repository](https://github.com/eochandler/predictive-maintenance-portfolio).

## Why This Project

Alongside the Olist BI Dashboard, this project rounds out the general-analytics side of this portfolio: churn prediction is one of the most common real-world classification problems across nearly every subscription or recurring-revenue business, and pairing a model with an explicit dollar-cost framework — rather than stopping at an accuracy score — is what makes a model's output actionable to a non-technical stakeholder.
